brief: How to raise your rates without losing the client

slots.subtitle: Not a number. Six levers that change what a client thinks they are buying, and what each one is worth in practice.
slots.issueLabel: The uncomfortable part is on the last page

slots.body: Selling time invites a comparison to every other person selling time. Selling an outcome removes the comparison entirely, because nobody else is offering exactly that.
slots.pillar1Body: Not the deliverable. A brand system is a service; being recognisable in your market is an outcome.
slots.pillar2Body: Partial scope invites partial payment. Take the seam and you take the value of closing it.
slots.pillar3Body: Ask what the situation is worth once it is fixed. Your cost to fix it is irrelevant to that number.
slots.quoteText: The hourly rate is a ceiling you build yourself.

slots.body: A single price is a yes-or-no question, and no is always the safer answer. Three options change the conversation from whether to which.
slots.pillar1Body: The top option is not there to be chosen. It is there to make the middle one look measured.
slots.pillar2Body: This is the one you actually want. Everything about it should read as the sensible choice.
slots.pillar3Body: A cheap option you would resent delivering will poison the work. Price it so you would be content.
slots.quoteText: Which, not whether — that is the whole shift.

slots.body: Every unbilled hour started as an assumption nobody wrote down. The exclusions protect the relationship more than the inclusions do.
slots.pillar1Body: Unlimited revisions is not generosity, it is a promise you will quietly start to resent.
slots.pillar2Body: Agreeing a rate for out-of-scope work in advance turns an argument into an invoice.
slots.pillar3Body: A quote with no expiry is a quote you will honour in a year at today's confidence.
slots.quoteText: Scope creep is a documentation failure, not a client failure.

slots.body: The silence after a price feels much longer to you than to them. Filling it is how a rate gets discounted before anyone has objected.
slots.pillar1Body: Hedging language tells the other side the number is negotiable before they have decided whether it is.
slots.pillar2Body: Explaining the number invites a line-by-line argument about the parts of it.
slots.pillar3Body: The first person to speak after a price is usually the one who moves on it.
slots.quoteText: Most discounts are self-inflicted in the pause.

slots.body: Asking for money before starting is standard everywhere except in the heads of people who have never asked. It also filters out the clients who were never going to pay.
slots.pillar1Body: It funds the work and it proves the intent. Both parties behave differently afterwards.
slots.pillar2Body: Payment on completion means you are financing the client at zero interest.
slots.pillar3Body: Never enforced, always effective. The clause does the work on its own.
slots.quoteText: Nobody has ever walked away over a deposit who would have paid the invoice.

slots.body: Positioning raises what people will pay for a given standard. It does not raise the standard, and a client who feels overcharged does not come back or refer you.
slots.pillar1Body: Charge above what you deliver and the market corrects it within about two projects.
slots.pillar2Body: Your real rate is whatever your last happy client tells someone you are worth.
slots.pillar3Body: Increase with each project until you feel resistance. That edge is the actual number.
slots.quoteText: Pricing is a lagging indicator of the work.

slots.body: Not on your current clients, and not by an amount you have to justify. On the next proposal, quietly, and see whether anyone objects.
